author: faassen
parent: (story) Is sandboxing sufficient to contain rogue agents?
text:
I've thought about this for a while in the context of coding agents.

My conclusion: if you have a rogue coding agent, it will find a way to escape, because fundamentally you want to be able to execute the code it writes, and an adversarial review of all the code it writes would be a LOT of work.

Besides this there are other escape vectors if you share write access to, say, the project directory: it can install some rogue code in a git hook which you then execute outside of the sandbox, for instance. Or, say, open your editor, or run build tools, etc. You can prevent this vector by having a coding agent commit separately from within the sandbox, which can create quite a bit of friction.

This is separate from limiting the damage of a coding agent mistake; there a sandbox is of great value.

So for a coding agent I'd focus on minimizing the chances a prompt causes it to go rogue - for instance by limiting network access. And of course to reduce the chances of prompt injection succeeding in the first place. The "Gray Swan" benchmark as shown here in the google gemini 4 argon announcement is interesting. Google is proud to say they only have a 0.7 percent chance a prompt injection attack succeeds after 15 attempts. That still means a lot of attacks do succeed!

author: Corbin
parent: (story) Prompting 101: Show, don’t tell
text:
Fairly good advice. It's also an example of good writing advice in general. Write for the prompt you want; if you want an expert sysadmin then give them part of a Linux kernel log and systemd output which is realistic but tailored for the scenario at hand. If you want them to ask for permission before doing things then don't put "username: root" in there, and pick usernames which are likely to be matched to the behaviors that you want; you can encourage them to sudo or doas instead by giving an example of proper usage. If you want them to think that they work for an elite corporation then display a banner which matches the ethical and ideological values that such a corporation would embody, and you should ensure that the details are likely to immerse the reader.

You can one-shot the example behavior (conversational, short lines, light punctuation) by prompting for e.g. an IRC conversation on any non-RL'd local model of the past 3yrs. This means that the model's context starts with the IRC client header and is followed by a fake OFTC/Freenode/etc. banner, a fake /join, a fake /topic, and synthesized timestamps before every message. After a fake /names, the model can be grammatically restricted to only use (its) real usernames, and a hard token cutoff can be used to interrupt run-on statements just like real IRC. We only enter the room with whatever we choose to bring into it.

text:
Posts like these have had me thinking recently about what makes art good. Art in this case being things we create because they give us purpose, like the author's retrocomputing project.

My working theory is that good art is original. Which means something that (1) no one else has done before or (2) no one else can do.

So for (1) someone can appreciate Starry Night as painted by Van Gogh, but if I make a perfect copy of it they're probably not going to be as impressed. It's not simply the painting itself that is an achievement --- the art exists in the context of our society. For (2), if someone thinks a water fountain is amazing, they probably would still be amazed if I were to make an exact copy of it, simply because making water fountains is hard.

(I think these qualities are not binary: this someone might still be impressed if you could perfectly recreate Starry Night if it were hard e.g. in the time before cameras)

The author's retrocomputing project's value as art laid chiefly in (2) --- this is not to say that no one can do it, but it needs time and care that no one but the author will put in. Now with the advent of LLMs, simply thinking "what if we had X" is basically enough to (possibly) create X. (There are people who will appreciate the craftsmanship, and I agree that a drive-by LLM creation will likely lack a "human touch," but it still dilutes the value of the final human product IMO) So what began as a quest for the author to create X now feels hollow.


I think this also explains why AI-generated menus and websites aren't as impressive as they might initially seem. Let's be generous and assume that they are aesthetically better than whatever came before. The problem is that now everyone is making them and the LLM tells are becoming obvious. So we're in a world where (a) we (think we) can tell apart a beautiful LLM menu and a beautiful human menu and (b) making the beautiful LLM menu is a prompt away. If everyone could summon Van Gogh to paint them some variation of Starry Night --- and they then hung them up in their living rooms --- something would be lost by the time you see the fiftieth Starryish Night.

My suspicion is that art will persevere by pushing further into the "out of distribution." I presume this is already what happens with the avant garde. It will be a sad day if we ever cease creating what the machine cannot.

I don't think writing software with a tool that imposes a constraint by construction means you don't understand the constraint. The reason the post ignores the economy of learning is because that's not the goal of the post.  If I were to unpack every counterargument that one might raise then the post would be incoherent and unfocused.  I usually try to write posts that explain one thing and explain it well and then subsequent posts can build upon ideas introduced in previous posts.

I've reviewed many agentically-coded pull requests and given feedback asking for small cleanups like "could you factor out this duplicate code into a shared function" or "could you split this out into a separate module".  Most would oblige, unsurprisingly, because they have an agent to do this drudgery for them; I heartily approve!

However, a couple of these agentic coders would consistently push back against the cleanup requests.  They wouldn't object to these requests on the merits; rather, they would portray the small refactor as an extraordinary imposition.  This initially caught me by surprise since I thought they could just forward the request to their agent, but eventually I began to learn that no amount of technology can save a person who loses faith in their own self-efficacy


Coding with a model might work for a bit, but as your own skills atrophy and you lose confidence in your ability to do the task or even review the model's output the more you will become unable to properly drive the model and then you end up helpless like the latter group of agentic coders.  That's where the economics of agentic coding fare poorly.
